logline: A reluctant con artist goes on the run from the FBI and her ruthless mob mother-in-law after a multimillion-dollar heist unravels overnight.

renewal.note: A seven-episode limited series adapted from Marissa Stapley's 2021 novel of the same name. The first two episodes premiered July 15, 2026, with the remaining five releasing weekly on Apple TV through the finale on August 19. No continuation has been announced.

bollymeter.basis: 79% on Rotten Tomatoes from 52 critics and 67 on Metacritic from 28 critics, with reviews genuinely split: Variety and The Daily Beast praised the chase mechanics and Anya Taylor-Joy's performance, while The Hollywood Reporter called it a series that 'never clicks, despite a strong cast.'

pull_quotes.text: An entertaining bit of thrilling fare that often promises more than it can deliver but never lets the audience down
Replete with gunfights, car chases and more than a few intriguing grifts, all seven episodes of Lucky feature heart-racing sequences
Never clicks, despite a strong cast.

seasons.review_body: Lucky lands on Apple TV as a seven-episode crime thriller, adapting Marissa Stapley's novel through creator Jonathan Tropper's lens, its first two hours dropping July 15 and the rest arriving weekly through August 19. The numbers split down the middle: 79 percent positive across 52 critics on Rotten Tomatoes against a cooler 67 from Metacritic's 28, and reading both sets of reviews explains the gap. Anya Taylor-Joy's con artist Lucky Armstrong, sprinting from Annette Bening's mob boss Priscilla and Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor's dogged FBI agent, generates real momentum in pure chase mechanics; Taylor-Joy and Timothy Olyphant, as Lucky's imprisoned father, do the season's heaviest lifting. The structural problem is the heist that starts everything happens off-screen before the pilot even begins, leaving the plotting to explain stakes it never earns. At seven episodes the show runs exactly long enough to expose how thin the supporting roles are.
